case_name: Centre de santé et de services sociaux de la Montagne v. E.S.
text:
Centre de santé et de services sociaux de la
Montagne v. E.S.

2013 QCCS
6131

JM1838

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-078207-134

DATE:

December 10, 2013

______________________________________________________________________

UNDER THE PRESIDENCY OF:

THE HONOURABLE

ROBERT MONGEON, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

CENTRE DE SANTÉ ET DE
SERVICES SOCIAUX DE LA MONTAGNE

Plaintiff

v.

E. S. (D.O.B.:  1959-[…])

Defendant

-and-

ES. S.

-and-

PUBLIC CURATOR OF QUEBEC

-and-

CENTRE MIRIAM

Mis-en-cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The Plaintiff Centre de Santé et des Services Sociaux de la Montagne
(CSSSM) seeks, at the request of the Public Curator of Quebec, an order of
lodging (Ordonnance d’Hébergement) with respect to Ms. E. S., aged 55 years
old.  Ms. S. is mentally retarded, severely affected with chronic diabetes and
diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.

[
2
]

Ms. S.’s health problems are such that she cannot live alone and can no
longer continue to live with her mother Mrs. Es. S., aged 77 years old, because
of the latter’s behaviour towards her.

[
3
]

For greater convenience, and most certainly not with a view to showing
disrespect, the Court will refer to Ms. E. S. as “E.” and to Mrs. Es. S., as
“Es.”.

[
4
]

For most of  her life, E. has lived with her mother.  However, her
relationship has always been one of dominant (Es.) towards submissive (E.).

[
5
]

E.’s current medical condition requires:

a)

a strict alimentary diet, otherwise she is at risks of falling into a
diabetic coma;

b)

a regular taking of her anti-psychotic medication (Risperdal) to control
her paranoid schizophrenia;

c)

proper care because of her mental handicap;

d)

a certain distance from the influence of her mother.

[
6
]

Es. is a very dominant and controlling person.  She has taken the habit
of treating E. as an underdog or “whipping boy”, thus abusing of E.’s own
weaknesses.

[
7
]

Following certain incidents (more fully described below), E. was removed
from the residence of her mother and temporarily placed in the care of a
“Ressource Intermédiaire”.  She now needs to be placed more permanently into a
public health care facility.

[
8
]

However, E. does not understand fully what is going on and is incapable
of giving, or refusing to give, an enlightened consent to her placement in such
facility.

[
9
]

Her incapacity is such that she is not fully aware of her medical
condition, is unable to understand the necessity of her placement and does not
realize that if she keeps on living with her mother, her health and security
are in danger.

[
10
]

In addition, her condition is permanent and irreversible.

[
11
]

Finally, E. is under the tutorship and curatorship of the Public
Curator, who has been impleaded in the present proceedings.  The Public Curator
who consents to the Motion of CSSSM and is in agreement with its conclusion.

THE FACTS
AND THE EVIDENCE

[
12
]

The record and the evidence adduced at hearing reveal the following
facts:

a)

E. was brought into the care of Centre Miriam after the discovery of
serious problems involving the behaviour of her mother, Es., towards her.

b)         On
or about July 12, 2013, Mrs. Toby Shainbaum-Pollak, a social worker at CSSS de
la Montagne, wrote the following report which was used to obtain the interim
placement order from Mr. Justice Peacock, on July 26, 2013.  The Report in
question is dated July 12, 2013 and is filed as Exhibit P-3.  The following
extracts are noteworthy:

Miss E. S., who will
be 54 years old next month, (Date of Birth:  1959-[…]) has an intellectual
handicap and is schizophrenic.  This report is written to request an emergency
permanent placement for E. and the protection of the public curator because her
current situation places E.’s safety and well-being at risk.

E. currently lives
with her 78-year-old mother, Mrs. Es. S..  Mrs. S. was diagnosed with paranoid
delusions in 2009.  E.’s father died about ten years ago.  Tragically, E.’s
younger sister, El. S., who was also intellectually handicapped, died in
September 2012, when she was struck by a maintenance vehicle.  There are no
other family members or friends who might care for E. on a daily basis.

E. has had a file with
CSSS de La Montagne since April 8, 1993,
and she has been employed by the
Jewish Employment Montreal JEM) Sheltered Workshop for thirty-two years.
During this time, it has often been observed that Mrs. S. is verbally abusive
to E., while favouring her other daughter
.  In the presence of JEM staff,
Miriam Home Readaptation Centre staff and CSSS workers, Mrs. S. has
called
E. denigrating names and insulted her
.  While this dynamic was concerning
to all,
E. has consistently stated that she would prefer to remain living
with her mother
.  Social work interventions were aimed at trying to improve
the family dynamic.

In addition to
concerns about E.’s emotional well-being, more recently, there have been
serious concerns about her physical well-being.  Most recently, E. appeared at
the JEM workshop on July 10, 2013,
with a swollen face, a cut between her
eyes and a swollen lip.
Her story about what happened was inconsistent.
She initially stated that her mother fell and paramedics came to the house.
She later stated that she fell and subsequently claimed that she hit a cupboard
(a previous story from another time she came to work with her head cut and
bloody).
It is highly significant that when a co-worker in the sheltered
workshop asked her what happened, E. answered:  “I fell, no one hit me.”  It
appeared that she was trying to follow her mother’s instructions not to
disclose what had happened.
This incident is not the first time what there
have been signs of physical abuse.  It is the agreement of the JEM workshop
staff, this social worker and the public curator that we cannot allow this
situation to escalate any further.  There is a serious possibility that if E.
is not placed, she could continue to face similar assaults at the hand of her
mother.

The use of violence
has been difficult to detect because E. has generally denied it and given
plausible explanations for her injuries.
On one occasion, in May 2013,
however, she did disclose to her Social Counselor at the sheltered workshop
that
her mother punches and kicks her
.  In May 2013, in the presence of
two JEM staff people, (after her Social Counselor, Ms. Gail Krasner, discussed
the fact that E. is not consistently taking the medication she requires for her
mental health), Mrs. S.
verbally and physically assaulted E.
.
Mrs.
S. was observed hitting and kicking E..
Mrs. S. told E. that she belongs in
her dead sister’s grave and that her sister should be alive instead of her.
Shelter staff tried to help Mrs. S. stop this abusive behaviour toward her
daughter.  It seems that this abuse is escalating.

(emphasis added)

c)

Expertise of Dr. Sylvain Louis Lafontaine

Dr. Lafontaine is a psychiatrist.  He has
examined E. and has delivered a detailed opinion
[1]

of her condition.  Dr. Lafontaine proceeded to a mental examination of E. and
concluded as follows:

Conclusion
:

The
main conclusion which is at the core of Ms. S.’s condition is that she has no
idea whatsoever of her medical condition, of the need to be treated, of the
danger of not following a strict treatment and here I am specifically thinking
about the treatment for her diabetes.
In such a context it is clear that
Ms. S. is unable to consent to her lodging.

She
is unable to take care of herself and she visibly shows, most of the time, a
psychotic behaviour.  This behaviour is covered by her mother’s own behaviour
and by her mother’s intrusiveness in Ms. S.’s life and her control over her
daughter in all aspect of her life.

Ms.
S. is under the dominance of her mother.  Mother acted in the same way with her
daughter L. to the point that in the past a psychiatrist described this as
“folie à deux”.
The psychotic bond between mother and daughter which makes
the two of them living out of the reality and therefore denying Ms. S.’s
condition and well being.  In fact, it is my opinion that Ms. S.’s mother is
using her daughter for her own psychological equilibrium and by doing so puts
her daughter in immediate danger.
She would do everything to stay with her
daughter even though this would put her daughter in danger because of her
medical condition.

But
both of them don’t understand her medical condition especially why to
administer treatment meaning the insulin treatment.

The
pathological relationship between the two is explained by the dynamic of the
relationship which is of a psychotic nature
.  This means that the mother
denies her daughter’s pathology its consequences and its threat to avoid
recognizing to her own self her own psychotic condition.  So more specifically,

the mother who is psychotic projects her psychosis into her daughter in
order to deny her own psychosis and her daughter is caught up with the mother
putting into herself psychotic elements.

The
paranoid nature of the illness is revealed by the delusion shared by both
daughter and mother that her other daughter was murdered.  In addition Ms. S.’s
intellectual handicap renders her more vulnerable to such indoctrination.

Diagnosis
:

In my
opinion, Ms. E. S. suffers from
paranoid schizophrenia.

I
explained above that
Ms. S. does not understand the need of a specific
lodging and even lodging which would be specifically aimed at controlling her
medical condition has been proposed and explained to her but she has refused.

This refusal in my opinion is the direct consequence of her mother’s action
upon her daughter to make her deny her psychotic condition and to make her deny
her medical condition as well.

Because
of Ms. S.’s psychotic condition, mainly her paranoid schizophrenia and because
she caught up in a psychotic relationship with her mother which
could be
labelled as “folie à deux” it is my opinion that she has no capacity to consent
to care, to consent to lodging and to consent to her future
.

(emphasis added)

d)

Observations of Ms. Melanie Reis and Toby Shainbaum-Pollak during the
supervised visits of Es. with E. over the last few months

E. was placed
in a foster home in July 2013 following an interim order of my colleague Mr.
Justice Mark G. Peacock.  Since then, Es. has been visiting E. as well as
speaking with her by telephone several times per week.  All these visits have
been supervised.  Mrs. Reis is a Social Worker who effected a substantial
portion of this supervision.  Her notes have been filed as Exhibit       P-8B.

In a combined
report dated October 31, 2013
[2]
,
Ms. Reis and her supervisor, Ms.Toby Shainbaum-Pollak, stated the following:

…

Social
work intervention has focused on trying to maintain the mother-daughter
relationship by offering supervised visits, while trying to ensure E.’s
psychological and physical well-being.  Community integration through arranging
attendance at synagogue and participation in community events has been an
important part of our social work intervention.
Ultimately, our social work
intervention will continue to try to support E.’s return to the Jewish
Employment Montreal sheltered workshop as this resource ensures that E. spends
her days more productively, but at this time E. refuses to return to the
workshop.  This refusal stems from E.’s mother regularly reiterating that E.
should not return to the workshop
.  Other community activities offered by
the YM-YWHA and Miriam Home were introduced and although E. was very happy to
participate in activities at the Y initially, since her mother told her that
the people there are “too low for her”, she declared to the group home manager
that she will not return.  (October 20, 2013, following telephone call with her
mother.)

Mrs.
S. states that she would accept E.’s involvement in social activities with
Miriam Home if E. returned to her care.  It should be noted that she withdrew
her other daughter from Miriam Home activities in the past
, preferring that
her daughter remain home with her, such that it is unclear if Mrs. S. would
follow through on this verbal agreement if E. were in her care.
It is
noteworthy that Mrs. S. already is sabotaging E.’s involvement in community
activities at the Y
.

Physical
well-being and medical concerns

In
the first 48 hours of E.’s placement at the residence, she appeared weak,
incontinent for urine and feces, and when her blood glucose level was tested,
it was determined to be dangerously high.  E. was sent by ambulance to the
Jewish General Hospital emergency room and she was admitted with pneumonia,
poorly controlled diabetes and a problem with her kidney function.  After stabilization,
E. returned to the residence.

While
at the residence, E.’s glucose levels have been well controlled as she is
following an appropriate diet.  She has also achieved a much healthier weight.
It is evident that E.’s diet was not as controlled when in her mother’s care.
…  E. has informed her mother that she now eats low-fat food and should not eat
sweets.  Despite this and repeated discussions about E.’s dietary requirements,
during supervised visits, Mrs. S. put a chocolate in her daughter’s mouth
(August 7, 2013), gave E. a lollipop and candied nuts which she falsely stated
were nuts without sugar (October 1, 2013), offered E. a chocolate croissant
(September 17, 2013) and has suggested that if her daughter were not in
placement, “E. would be free and would have no police to watch her” (September
10, 2013).  Mrs. S. stated that she does not believe that E.’s diabetes is
influenced at all by what she eats (October 1, 2013).

…
Mrs. S. seems completely unaware of the serious nature
of E.’s diabetic condition
.  She described that if her daughter were living
with her, she would be free to go to the baker or shopping mall courts to eat
without supervision (September 10, 2013).  She recently proposed that E. should
fast for Yom Kippur, a Jewish religious fast day (September 10, 2013).  This
would be dangerous to E.’s health and even Jewish religious authorities would
not advocate that a person with diabetes fast.

…

…“
When
E. is nice, I stop the Risperdal” (October 17, 2013).
Although it was
explained to the mother and E. that the medication helps E. to function well,
Mrs. S. communicated that she was not convinced.

…

…it
was stated that there were serious concerns about E.’s safety and that we could
not allow anyone to hurt her.  E.’s response was to state:  “
my mother
doesn’t hurt me anymore
” (August 10, 2013).  This reply is quite
significant because it
supports the allegations that Mrs. S. has hurt her
daughter in the past.

…

During
supervised visits, the mother complained frequently about how she has been
negatively affected by her daughter’s placement.  She shared with her daughter
that she feels alone and has no one to prepare her breakfast.  Mrs. S. has
stated:  “
I’m miserable without you.  I need you to help me.” (September 17,
2013).  The emphasis in many of the mother-daughter conversations was on Mrs.
S.’s own needs
.  Furthermore, it seems that Mrs. S. is pressuring E. to
come home to take care of her as though this placement is of E.’s own volition.

…

Mrs.
S. was quite upset that E.’s paycheques from the work period prior to the
placement were not sent to her
.  She was quite insistant that these funds
belong to her.  As noted in the previous court report, Mrs. S. has a long
history of instructing E. as to what position she should take, rather than permitting
her daughter to express her own point of view.  In one supervised visit, Mrs.
S. asked E. if she was happy at the Miriam Home Residence.  When E. answered
that she is happy, Mrs. S. responded “So you’re not happy and you want to come
home with me” (August 20, 2013).

…

Mrs.
S. has used her nightly telephone contact with E. to coach her daughter about
what she should say to her lawyer, the Public Curator, the consulting
psychiatrist and during this court appearance.  After the telephone
conversations, the group home manager hears E. repeating what she is supposed
to say.  During a supervised visit (October 8, 2013), Mrs. S. instructed E. and
E. obliged by repeating her mother’s discourse a few times.  On October 17,
2013, Mrs. S. screamed at E. to “shut up” when E. repeated too many times what
her mother wanted her to say.  It must be stated that it is difficult to know
what E. truly wants as she has been made to repeat her mother’s words so
frequently.

(emphasis added)

[
13
]

These observations led to the following:

…

Mrs. Es. S. is in her
late 70’s and has some health issues herself, including a previous diagnosis of
paranoid delusions (2009) that remains untreated.  Certainly, as Mrs. S. gets
older, it has been more challenging for her to care for her daughter.  While
she would like E. to go to a Miriam Home placement one day, Mrs. S. would like
this to be at a time of her own choosing in the future.

This report has
highlighted that E.’s physical and psychological well-being are in jeopardy
when in her mother’s care. …
Mrs. S. undermines those professionals who are
able to enhance E.’s quality of life.  Her regular telephone contacts are used
to instruct E. to avoid activities that are actually beneficial to E.
.
Accordingly, all mother-daughter contact should not only be monitored, but
should also be
terminated if Mrs. S. is unable to be appropriate.

While E. prefers to
return to her mother’s home, she has made a positive adaptation to the Miriam
home resource.  Furthermore, plans have been established to ensure an improved
social-therapeutic integration in the future.

Accordingly, it is
strongly recommended that the court orders a continued placement with Miriam
Home Services.

(emphasis added)

e)

Observation of Sherri Gutberg,
Social Worker

Ms. Gutberg
is a Social Worker.  She has performed a psycho-social evaluation of E. (P-9).
Her remarks as to the physical condition of E. upon her arrival at the
“Ressource Intermédiaire” on July 23, 2013 is quite significant:

E. was placed in a
Miriam Home RI on July 23
rd
, 2013.  On July 26
th
, the
home managers expressed to this worker that they observed that E. appeared very
weak, and was incontinent for urine and feces which seemed unusual for her.
Later in the day, the home manager had taken E.’s sugar level knowing that she
is diabetic and confirmed that E.’s sugar level was 29.0 which was excessively
high.  Knowing that E.’s sugar level was dangerously high, 911 was called and
E. was taken to the Jewish General Hospital.  E. was seen in the Emergency Room
at the JGH where doctors admitted her as it was confirmed that E. had
Pneumonia, a poor functioning kidney and poorly controlled diabetes.

[
14
]

This was the direct result of Es.’s lack of proper care of E..  In point
of fact, E. was more or less left to manage her medication by herself although
she lacked the necessary knowledge and understanding to do so.

[
15
]

Mrs. Gutberg’s conclusions are as follows:

This social worker became involved in E.’s file
after she was placed at the Miriam Home RI on July 23rd, 2013.  The day after
E. was placed, the home manager noted that she appeared very weak and was
incontinent for urine and bowels which seemed unusual for her.  E. continues to
appear ill and an ambulance was called on July 26th when her sugar level was
excessively high.  Medical staff at the JGH confirmed that E. had a urinary
tract infection, poorly functioning kidney and poor controlled diabetes.  Given
that E. needed to be admitted to hospital within 72 hours of being placed at
the RI, demonstrates that she must have been ill prior to entering the RI, and
concludes that E.’s mother is no longer capable of taking proper care of her.

On August 5
th
, 2013 E. was medically
stable and discharged from the Jewish General Hospital.  Since returning back
to the RI, E. appears happy in the home, and is visited by residential
educator, Patrick Gilkes on a regular basis.  Patrick reports that E. is doing
well at the RI and has been going on regular outings.  E. continues to
verbalize that she does not want to return to work.  These verbalizations
happen after phone calls with her mother who is adamant that she not return to
JEM.  E. had stated an interest in participating in community recreational
activities, but after several discussions with her mother she has verbalized that
she is no longer interested in participating.

Given that E. has now been in placement at the RI
for a period of 90 days, and doing fairly well overall, the following is
therefore recommended:

•

That E. return to work or participate in full time structured
recreational activities.

•

That E. remain in placement on a permanent basis, where her
medical and psychological needs will be met.

•

For E. to continue to have a relationship with her mother.
Miriam Home can supervise visits between E. and her mother every two weeks.
These visits will be re-evaluated every three months.  E. can continue to speak
to her mother three times a week for a fifteen minute period.  These calls will
be monitored by the home manager.

•

The RI address should not be disclosed to Mrs. S..

[
16
]

Based upon the foregoing, the CSSSM seeks the authorization of this
Court to place E. in a lodging resource for three years, even against the will
of E., in order to ensure the regular taking of her medication and other proper
supervision of her activities, the whole with a view to providing better living
conditions for this person.

[
17
]

One of the obvious drawbacks of this plan is the quasi-total separation
of E. from her mother, while it is expected that such separation will continue
to perturbe the life of both E. and her mother.

[
18
]

Both E. and Es. were heard in contestation of the position of the CSSSM.

[
19
]

E. expresses herself quite clearly.  She understands the questions, and
she provides answers directly related to the questions put to her.  Her mental
handicap is apparent but not to a point of depriving her of all her capacity to
reason.

[
20
]

E. states that she does not find her actual lodging conditions very
comfortable.  They are, as she puts it, “
very loud
”.

[
21
]

She wants to go back and live with her mother.  “
She is missing me
”,
she says.

[
22
]

E. is very concerned that if she does not go back, her mother will have
nobody to look after her and will go back to Tel Aviv where she has relatives.
Her fear of having her mother in Israel is overwhelming.  “
I will be all
alone here
”, she says.

[
23
]

E. understands that she is diabetic and that there are certain foods
that she cannot eat, otherwise her health could be severally affected.

[
24
]

She does not clearly understand the fact that she suffers from paranoid
schizophrenia.  She knows that she must take Risperdal but not why.

[
25
]

E. is very concerned about the possibility of her mother moving back to
Israel.  In point of fact, she clearly states that she wants to go back and
live with her mother, only because she wishes to prevent her mother from
departing and permanently moving to Israel.  Such a scenario would be
catastrophic to E..  She has lived with her mother all her life except during
the last four months and her mother is her only family here.

[
26
]

E. seems to be more concerned with taking all necessary ways and means
to keep her mother near her, even at the risk of continuing to endure her
mother’s dominance.

[
27
]

Es. also testified.

[
28
]

Contrary to the testimony of her daughter, Es. wants her to come back
and live with her in order to have E. look after her rather than her looking
after E..

[
29
]

Es. does not want to live alone:  …”
Who’s going to look after me
?”…,
she says.

[
30
]

She wants her daughter with her mainly to ensure her own comfort.  …”
What
have I done to God not to have my daughter with me?
”…, she says.

[
31
]

Es. only wants to protect herself and does not show much empathy towards
looking at the well-being of E..

[
32
]

On the other hand, it would seem that the separation of mother and
daughter has caused and is causing much distress and insecurity with both of them.

[
33
]

The testimony of E. and of her mother Es. reveal that they are, and will
be in the future, seriously affected by this separation although Es.’s
preoccupations are centered around her own well-being and not towards the
proper care of E.’s needs.

DISCUSSION

[
34
]

Both mother and daughter are sick and are in serious need of medical
treating and caring for E. will solve only one portion of the problem.  On the
other hand, the Court has jurisdiction on E. and not on Es..

[
35
]

The first and foremost role of the Court is to render in the best
interest of E..

[
36
]

Articles 11 and following of the
Civil Code of Quebec
provide:

Art. 11.  No person
may be made to undergo care of any nature, whether for examination, specimen
taking, removal of tissue, treatment or any other act, except with his consent.

If the person
concerned is incapable of giving or refusing his consent to care, a person
authorized by law or by mandate given in anticipation of his incapacity may do
so in his place.

Art. 12.    A
person who gives
his consent to or refuses care for another person is bound to act in the sole
interest of that person, taking into account, as far as possible, any wishes
the latter may have expressed.

If he gives his
consent, he shall ensure that the care is beneficial notwithstanding the
gravity and permanence of certain of its effects, that it is advisable in the
circumstances and that the risks incurred are not disproportionate to the
anticipated benefit.

…

Art. 15.
Where
it is ascertained that a person of full age is incapable of giving consent to
care required by his or her state of health, consent is given by his or her
mandatary, tutor or curator. If the person of full age is not so represented,
consent is given by his or her married, civil union or
de facto
spouse
or, if the person has no spouse or his or her spouse is prevented from giving
consent, it is given by a close relative or a person who shows a special
interest in the person of full age.

Art. 16
.

The authorization of the court is necessary where the person who may give
consent to care required by the state of health of a minor or a person of full
age who is incapable of giving his consent is prevented from doing so or,
without justification, refuses to do so; it is also required where a person of
full age who is incapable of giving his consent categorically refuses to
receive care, except in the case of hygienic care or emergency.

The
authorization of the court is necessary, furthermore, to cause a minor 14 years
of age or over to undergo care he refuses, except in the case of emergency if
his life is in danger or his integrity threatened, in which case the consent of
the person having parental authority or the tutor is sufficient.

…

Art. 23.  When the
court is called upon to rule on an application for authorization with respect
to care or the alienation of a body part, it obtains the opinions of experts,
of the person having parental authority, of the mandatary, of the tutor or the
curator and of the tutorship council; it may also obtain the opinion of any
person who shows a special interest in the person concerned by the application.

The court is also
bound to obtain the opinion of the person concerned unless that is impossible,
and to respect his refusal unless the care is required by his state of health.

[
37
]

The notion of care includes the choice and supervision of lodging
facilities.  See:
CSSS Rimouski-Neigettes c. T.C.
,
2010, QCCA 143
;
CHUQ
c. L.R
.,
J.E. 2000-1984 (C.A.)
.

[
38
]

In the present context, E. is under full tutorship to the person and
curatorship to her property and assets.  Consequently, it could be open to the
Public Curator to consent to E.’s lodging and E. would have little or nothing
to say.  However, the Court believes that it must intervene when the person
involved strongly manifests her opposition, as it is the case here.

[
39
]

The Court is convinced that it is in the best interests of E. that she
stops living with her mother.  Furthermore, the Court is of the view that Es.
has a strong tendency of imposing her will upon her daughter, not for the
benefit of E. but for her own well-being.  In other words, not only must there
be a break in the cohabitation between mother and daughter but certain controls
must be put in place in order to reduce and/or eliminate the mother’s dominance
over her daughter.

[
40
]

On the other hand, these controls should not be so strict that the
communications and contacts between mother and daughter will become
non-existent to a point where their life-long relationship will be
annihilated.  It should not be forgotten that these two persons have, until
July 2013, always lived under the same roof and that they both need the support
and presence of each other.

[
41
]

Both E. and Es. do not fully understand why they are being separated.
Obviously, Es. is not in any way facilitating the situation.  In point of fact,
she is doing everything in her power to perturb the current and proposed
arrangement.

[
42
]

The Court believes that the limited contacts between mother and daughter
currently in place and suggested by the CSSSM are much too strict and go beyond
what is necessary or appropriate.

[
43
]

Es. may only speak to her daughter by telephone three times per week for
a maximum of fifteen minutes and only if an attendant from the CSSSM is
available to monitor the conversations.

[
44
]

E. may see her mother at Synagogue every week, before or after the
religious service and at community gatherings, but only if E. is accompanied by
a person who will make sure that Es. will  not offer food to E. susceptible of
affecting her health.

[
45
]

The interim order of Mr. Justice Peacock, still in force, does not allow
much contact between mother and daughter.  The interim order reads in part as
follows:

[17]      AUTHORIZES in emergency situations that
Mrs. Es. S. be advised of that emergency regarding Defendant and that she be
allowed to visit Defendant at the hospital under the supervision of hospital
staff;

[18]      ORDERS that visitation rights of Mrs.
Es. S. to Defendant be managed by Plaintiff, along with Centre Miriam, until
judgment on the merits;

[19]      ACKNOWLEDGES the undertaking by
Plaintiff to arrange bi-weekly visits of Mrs. Es. S. to Defendant, these visits
taking place under the supervision of an intervener designated by Plaintiff and
at a place designated by Plaintiff, until judgment on the merits;

[20]      ACKNOWLEDGES the undertaking by
Plaintiff to allow for a weekly visit of Mrs. Es. S. to Defendant, on Saturdays
as of August 3, 2013, on Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and Sukkot and on September 7
and 12, 2013, between 9:30 a.m. and 3:00 p.m., at the Spanish and Portuguese
Synagogue on St-Kevin, transportation of Defendant and supervision of visits
being ensured by a family friend or volunteer of the synagogue approved of by
Plaintiff, until judgment on the merits.

…

[23]      ACKNOWLEDGES the undertaking by Mrs.
Es. S. not to attend at the place of residence of Defendant, until judgment on
the merits;

[24]      ACKNOWLEDGES the undertaking by Mrs.
Es. S. to contact Plaintiff and not Centre Miriam for any questions or comments
regarding Defendant, except in case of emergency;

…

[27]      ACKNOWLEDGES the undertaking by Centre
Miriam to encourage daily outings of Defendant with interveners, until judgment
on the merits;

[
46
]

E.’s outings are also strictly controlled:

[25]      ORDERS that outings of Defendant be
managed by Centre Miriam, along with Plaintiff, until judgment on the merits;

[26]      ACKNOWLEDGES the undertaking by Centre
Miriam to allow outings of Defendant whenever she is supervised by a person
approved of by Centre Miriam, until judgment on the merits;

[
47
]

The undersigned is of the opinion that in an ideal world:

-

telephone calls between E. and her mother need not to be monitored.  E.
should be able to call her mother whenever she wants;

-

E. should be able to visit her mother at her home whenever she wants;

[
48
]

This ideal situation may not occur overnight.

[
49
]

The undersigned is of the view that E.’s rights would be better
protected if some reasonable hope could be given to her (and indirectly to her
mother) that they will not be separated forever without the possibility of
better quality contacts over time.  This does not mean that E. would return to
her mother’s residence to live there but she should, with time, be able to
speak to her mother without being observed and she should be able to visit her
mother without being accompanied.

[
50
]

Over a period of, say, 6 to 9 months, some measures could be put in
place to reduce the surveillance and allow more frequent and better contacts
between these two persons.

[
51
]

Month by month, with a certain progression, unsupervised telephone
conversations could be considered.

[
52
]

Month by month, certain unsupervised visits of E. at her mother’s
residence could be arranged, starting with short visits and increasing
frequency and length.

[
53
]

The Court acknowledges also that it is not an expert in these fields and
that the Court should not take initiatives without firstly seeking the advice
or recommendations of the doctors, nurses, social workers and other personnel
of the CSSSM looking after E..

[
54
]

On the other hand, a proposed plan of action could be put in place
progressively and if mother and daughter are given the opportunity of having
better quality contacts with each other, they may realize that it is in their
respective best interest to follow a progressive increase in the frequency and
quality of their contacts from now on.

[
55
]

The Court is not satisfied with the suggestion of simply replacing Mr.
Justice Peacock’s Interim Order with a permanent one for the next three years,
without a progressive “exit plan”, allowing for a better communication between
E. and her mother.

[
56
]

On the other hand, the Court believes that until such “exit plan” is put
together and ratified, the Order of Mr. Justice Peacock should continue to
apply.

[
57
]

The Court is of the view that the CSSSM should consider the opportunity
of putting an “exit plan” together whereby:

a)

E. would continue to reside in a “Ressource Intermédiaire” and not with
her mother;

b)

the supervision of every telephone call, every visit or every contact
between mother and daughter would progressively diminish with a view to
eliminating such supervision over a period of, say, six to nine months;

c)

in addition, unsupervised visits, contacts and telephone calls could be
allowed, progressively increasing in frequency and duration over the same
period of six to nine months, with a view to eliminating all restrictions
(except the residence requirement mentioned in (a) above).

[
58
]

The Court is of the view that the possibility of putting such “exit
plan” should be examined within the next 90 days and to further report to the
undersigned.  It is important to allow for a better form of contact between E. and
Es. more particularly if the risk of Es.’s departure for Israel becomes more
than a distant possibility.

[
59
]

Accordingly, this Court will postpone the Motion of the CSSSM to a date
to be determined in March 2014 and review the situation based on the recommendations
of the social workers and/or treating physicians before making a final order,
valid for the next three years.  In the interim, the Court:

[
60
]

RENEWS
and
CONTINUES
the interim Order of Mr. Justice Mark
Peacock for a period of ninety days, that is until March 5, 2014 at 1700 hours;

[
61
]

CONTINUES
the Motion “
pro forma
” before the undersigned
who will remain seized of this matter to March 5, 2014, at 0915 hours in a
Court Room to be determined; and in the interim,

[
62
]

REQUESTS
the CSSSM to examine the possibility of reviewing the
contacts, visits and communications between E. and Es. taking into account the
suggestions outlined in the above reasons and to furnish the Court with a
report of their recommendations.
